literature.title: SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
literature.abstract: We explore and enhance the ability of neural language models to generate novel scientific directions grounded in literature. Work on literature-based hypothesis generation has traditionally focused on binary link prediction— severely limiting the expressivity of hypotheses. This line of work also does not focus on optimizing novelty. We take a dramatic departure with a novel setting in which models use as input background contexts (e.g., problems, experimental settings, goals), and output natural language ideas grounded in literature. We present SCIMON, a modeling framework that uses retrieval of “inspirations” from past scientific papers, and explicitly optimizes for novelty by iteratively comparing to prior papers and updating idea suggestions until sufficient novelty is achieved. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that GPT-4 tends to generate ideas with overall low technical depth and novelty, while our methods partially mitigate this issue. Our work represents a first step toward evaluating and developing language models that generate new ideas derived from the scientific literature1.

literature.title: Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment of Scientific Ideas
literature.abstract: Automated scientific idea generation systems have made remarkable progress, yet the automatic evaluation of idea novelty remains a critical and underexplored challenge. Manual evaluation of novelty through literature review is labor-intensive, prone to error due to subjectivity, and impractical at scale. To address these issues, we propose the Idea Novelty Checker, an LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that leverages a two-stage retrieve-then-rerank approach. The Idea Novelty Checker first collects a broad set of relevant papers using keyword and snippet-based retrieval, then refines this collection through embedding-based filtering followed by facet-based LLM re-ranking. It incorporates expert-labeled examples to guide the system in comparing papers for novelty evaluation and in generating literature-grounded reasoning. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our novelty checker achieves approximately 13% higher agreement than existing approaches. Ablation studies further showcases the importance of the facet-based re-ranker in identifying the most relevant literature for novelty evaluation.

literature.title: Is This Idea Novel? An Automated Benchmark for Judgment of Research Ideas
literature.abstract: Judging the novelty of research ideas is crucial for advancing science, enabling the identification of unexplored directions, and ensuring contributions meaningfully extend existing knowledge rather than reiterate minor variations. However, given the exponential growth of scientific literature, manually judging the novelty of research ideas through literature reviews is labor-intensive, subjective, and infeasible at scale. Therefore, recent efforts have proposed automated approaches for research idea novelty judgment. Yet, evaluation of these approaches remains largely inconsistent and is typically based on non-standardized human evaluations, hindering large-scale, comparable evaluations. To address this, we introduce RINoBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for large-scale evaluation of research idea novelty judgments. It comprises 1,381 research ideas derived from and judged by human experts as well as nine automated evaluation metrics designed to assess both rubric-based novelty scores and textual justifications of novelty judgments. Using this benchmark, we evaluate several state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) on their ability to judge the novelty of research ideas. Our findings reveal that while LLM-generated reasoning closely mirrors human rationales, this alignment does not reliably translate into accurate novelty judgments, which diverge significantly from human gold standard judgments—even among leading reasoning-capable models. Data and code available at: https://github.com/TimSchopf/RINoBench. Keywords: research idea novelty judgment, evaluation benchmark, scientific discovery, llm-as-a-judge

literature.title: Think-Probe-Respond: Improving Large Language Models as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
literature.abstract: Automated novelty judgment can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling efficient evaluation, refinement, and comparison of research ideas. While large language models are increasingly adopted for this task, we investigate a previously overlooked limitation in their judgment capabilities: despite generating reasoning rationales that closely mirror those of human experts, their final novelty judgments often diverge substantially. We demonstrate that this miscalibration stems from a systematic bias towards judging ideas as “medium novel”. To mitigate this, we propose ThinkProbe-Respond (TPR), a lightweight approach that probes latent novelty judgments from hidden states during the reasoning phase and uses the probed judgments to condition the final response. Across strong baselines, TPR improves novelty judgment performance by 22.30% and successfully mitigates the prevalent “medium novelty” bias.

literature.title: Exploring the Design of Multi-Agent LLM Dialogues for Research Ideation
literature.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support creative tasks such as research idea generation. While recent work has shown that structured dialogues between LLMs can improve the novelty and feasibility of generated ideas, the optimal design of such interactions remains unclear. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of multi-agent LLM dialogues for scientific ideation. We compare different configurations of agent roles, number of agents, and dialogue depth to understand how these factors influence the novelty and feasibility of generated ideas. Our experimental setup includes settings where one agent generates ideas and another critiques them, enabling iterative improvement. Our results show that enlarging the agent cohort, deepening the interaction depth, and broadening agent persona heterogeneity each enrich the diversity of generated ideas. Moreover, specifically increasing critic-side diversity within the ideation–critique–revision loop further boosts the feasibility of the final proposals. Our findings offer practical guidelines for building effective multi-agent LLM systems for scientific ideation.

initial_idea.title: Mitigating Medium Novelty Bias in Multi-Agent Scientific Ideation via Latent Probing
initial_idea.research_problem: How can multi-agent scientific ideation frameworks overcome systematic biases in novelty judgment to generate truly high-impact research directions?
initial_idea.research_gap: While recent frameworks generate literature-grounded scientific ideas and assess novelty using retrieval and multi-agent dialogue, language models suffer from a pervasive "medium novelty" bias where their final judgments and iterative refinements diverge from human gold standards due to miscalibrated reasoning-to-judgment translation.
initial_idea.methodology: We propose a unified pipeline combining multi-agent ideation with a latent-probing calibration mechanism. During the generation and critique loop, where generator and critic agents iteratively refine research directions, we integrate a Think-Probe-Respond layer. Instead of allowing the model's final text generation to default to safe, medium-novelty compromises, we probe the hidden states during the critique phase to extract latent novelty judgments. These probed signals condition the final refinement prompt, steering the multi-agent system toward genuinely novel conceptual spaces.
initial_idea.expected_contribution: An integrated multi-agent scientific ideation framework that leverages latent probing to eliminate medium-novelty bias, yielding research directions with higher technical depth and verified novelty scores.
initial_idea.experimental_setup: We utilize the RINoBench benchmark and the SciMON generation task setup. We deploy a multi-agent ideation architecture consisting of diverse personas (generator, reviewer, domain expert) using frozen LLM APIs. We compare our latent-probe-enhanced multi-agent loop against standard multi-agent generation baselines and standalone SciMON configurations across 200 standard computer science research background contexts.
initial_idea.evaluation_strategy: We evaluate the generated ideas using RINoBench metrics and the Idea Novelty Checker framework. We measure alignment with human expert novelty judgments, distribution variance across novelty tiers to verify mitigation of the medium-novelty bias, and technical depth scores.
feasibility_assumptions: Access to standard LLM APIs for multi-agent generation and hidden state extraction.
Availability of the public RINoBench dataset for evaluation.
Feasibility of completing the 6-week project timeline without model weight training.

final_idea.title: Mitigating Medium Novelty Bias in Multi-Agent Scientific Ideation via Latent Probing and Prompt Conditioning
final_idea.research_problem: How can multi-agent scientific ideation frameworks overcome systematic medium-novelty biases in model reasoning to generate truly high-impact research directions?
final_idea.research_gap: While recent frameworks generate literature-grounded scientific ideas and assess novelty using retrieval and multi-agent dialogue, language models suffer from a pervasive medium novelty bias where their final judgments and iterative refinements diverge from human gold standards. Existing work like Think-Probe-Respond addresses this bias exclusively as a single-model evaluation task rather than an active multi-agent generation and steering mechanism, and lacks integration with iterative generation loops like SciMON.
final_idea.methodology: We propose an integrated multi-agent ideation pipeline incorporating latent-probe-based prompt conditioning. To adhere to hardware limits of a single 12GB consumer GPU within a 6-week timeline, we use locally hosted open-weights 4-bit quantized Llama-3-8B-Instruct models without full fine-tuning. Instead of unstable live runtime activation vector manipulation, we extract hidden states from the critic agent during its reasoning phase and apply offline-trained lightweight linear probes to predict explicit novelty tiers. The continuous probed novelty scores are mapped via a discrete translation function into natural prompt prefixes injected into the generator agent's context, pulling outputs away from safe medium-novelty compromises toward high-risk, high-reward conceptual spaces.
final_idea.expected_contribution: An integrated multi-agent scientific ideation framework leveraging open-weights hidden state probing and lightweight prompt-level conditioning to eliminate medium-novelty bias, yielding research directions with higher technical depth and verified novelty scores without requiring full LLM fine-tuning.
final_idea.experimental_setup: We utilize a representative subset of 50 background contexts drawn from the RINoBench benchmark and SciMON generation tasks to ensure compute feasibility. We deploy a multi-agent ideation architecture consisting of diverse personas (generator, reviewer, domain expert) using locally hosted Llama-3-8B-Instruct models. We compare our probe-enhanced multi-agent loop against standard multi-agent generation baselines, standalone SciMON configurations, a prompt-only novelty constraint text baseline, and classifier-guided decoding baselines.
final_idea.evaluation_strategy: We evaluate generated ideas using RINoBench metrics and the Idea Novelty Checker framework. We measure alignment with human expert novelty judgments, distribution variance across novelty tiers to verify mitigation of medium-novelty bias, technical depth scores, and computational footprint analysis tracking latency and memory overhead on the consumer GPU. We also include a falsification baseline to verify whether prompt conditioning yields actual technical depth rather than superficial lexical novelty.
feasibility_assumptions: Access to locally hosted open-weights models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) compatible with a 12GB consumer GPU via 4-bit quantization.
Availability of public RINoBench dataset and SciMON benchmark contexts for evaluation.
Feasibility of completing the 6-week project timeline using frozen base weights and offline-trained lightweight linear probes without full LLM fine-tuning.
Reliance on discrete prompt conditioning derived from a robust fallback mapping function to maintain semantic coherence and avoid VRAM bottlenecks.

review.explanation: The proposal aims to mitigate medium-novelty bias in multi-agent scientific ideation by combining multi-agent generation with latent probing. However, the core technique of 'Think-Probe-Respond' (TPR) for mitigating medium-novelty bias via hidden-state extraction and probing was very recently introduced by Schopf et al. (2026.findings-emnlp.574). Directly transferring this technique from novelty evaluation to multi-agent ideation generation represents an incremental application rather than a conceptually novel breakthrough. Furthermore, the proposal relies heavily on combining existing frameworks (SciMON, RINoBench, Idea Novelty Checker, and Think-Probe-Respond) without introducing a fundamentally new architectural mechanism for ideation itself.
problems: The proposed 'Think-Probe-Respond' calibration mechanism directly mirrors the recently published TPR method by Schopf et al. (2026.findings-emnlp.574), lowering the conceptual novelty of the core methodological contribution.

The proposal combines existing tools (SciMON for ideation, Idea Novelty Checker for retrieval-based evaluation, RINoBench for benchmarks, and TPR for probing) without offering a novel paradigm for multi-agent interaction dynamics beyond standard generation-critique loops.

Extracting and probing hidden states from commercial frozen LLM APIs (as noted in the feasibility assumptions) is technically restricted or impossible for many proprietary models like GPT-4, posing a severe mismatch between the methodology and the stated API reliance.
improvements: Redefine the probing mechanism to operate on open-weight models (e.g., Llama-3) where hidden states are fully accessible, and design a novel multi-agent latent feedback loop rather than directly porting a single-model judge calibration method.

Differentiate the generation-phase bias correction from existing evaluation-phase bias correction (Schopf et al., 2026) by introducing active latent reward steering during token decoding rather than simple prompt conditioning.
Incorporate novel multi-agent persona structures that explicitly target the generation of high-risk, high-reward conceptual leaps rather than relying solely on standard generator-reviewer roles.

review.explanation: The proposal presents a well-structured and highly practical methodology suited for a 6-week academic timeframe, leveraging open-weights quantized models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) fitting within a 12GB consumer GPU. By substituting expensive activation steering with discrete prompt prefix conditioning derived from lightweight linear probes on critic hidden states, the project respects hardware constraints. However, training and evaluating linear probes simultaneously while orchestrating a multi-agent loop over 200 diverse benchmark contexts within 6 weeks leaves very little margin for error, particularly regarding data collection for probe training.
problems: Training linear probes for latent space novelty classification requires a sufficient collection of hidden states paired with labeled novelty tiers from intermediate reasoning steps, which adds data collection overhead.
Running multi-agent generation loops across 200 background contexts using an 8B model on a single consumer GPU may suffer from accumulated inference latency within a tight 6-week timeline.
Prompt prefix injection from continuous probe scores may lead to syntactic instability or degraded semantic coherence if not carefully calibrated.
improvements: Reduce the evaluation set size from 200 to a representative subset of 50 background contexts to ensure sufficient compute time for probe training and ablation studies within the 6-week window.
Pre-collect hidden states and train the linear probes offline on a fixed dataset rather than training them dynamically inside the multi-agent generation loop.
Implement a fallback discrete mapping function for probe scores to ensure prompt prefixes remain linguistically natural.

review.explanation: The proposal aims to bridge a compelling gap by extending latent-space probing (originally demonstrated for single-model novelty evaluation in Think-Probe-Respond) into an active multi-agent generation loop. However, the core mechanism rests on a shaky translational bridge: extracting a linear probe score from a critic's internal states during text generation and converting it into a discrete text prompt or prefix token for a separate generator model. This setup assumes that a latent representation tuned to judge novelty in one agent can cleanly guide the creative output of another quantized, distinct persona without inducing catastrophic semantic drift or prompt degradation. Furthermore, attempting to manage multi-agent loops, hidden state extraction, linear probe training, and generation on a single 12GB consumer GPU within a 6-week timeline introduces severe resource friction.
problems: The translation mechanism from continuous latent probe scores to discrete prompt conditioning tokens is ad-hoc and lacks theoretical grounding for steering creative generation rather than passive classification.

Probing hidden states of quantized 8B models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) across multi-agent loops on a 12GB VRAM consumer GPU creates major memory swapping and throughput bottlenecks, conflicting with the feasibility assumptions.
The proposal assumes that a linear probe trained on critic reasoning states can reliably steer a separate generator model, ignoring the discrepancy in persona-specific latent geometries.

Failure mode: The prompt conditioning mechanism may simply force superficial buzzwords associated with 'high novelty' into the text without increasing actual technical depth or logical grounding, bypassing true conceptual innovation.
improvements: Replace the discrete prompt prefix injection with a lightweight decoding-time guidance strategy (such as classifier-guided generation) directly on the generator logits to test if latent signals can steer token probabilities more reliably than text prompts.
Narrow the scope to a single-model iterative refinement loop (akin to SciMON or standalone Think-Probe-Respond) before attempting a multi-agent distributed setup on a single 12GB GPU.

Provide a concrete falsification experiment showing that the probe-conditioned generator actually produces ideas that outperform a simpler text-only style baseline on expert evaluation metrics rather than superficial lexical novelty.

revised_idea.title: Mitigating Medium Novelty Bias in Multi-Agent Scientific Ideation via Latent Probing and Prompt Conditioning
revised_idea.research_problem: How can multi-agent scientific ideation frameworks overcome systematic medium-novelty biases in model reasoning to generate truly high-impact research directions?
revised_idea.research_gap: While recent frameworks generate literature-grounded scientific ideas and assess novelty using retrieval and multi-agent dialogue, language models suffer from a pervasive medium novelty bias where their final judgments and iterative refinements diverge from human gold standards. Existing work like Think-Probe-Respond addresses this bias exclusively as a single-model evaluation task rather than an active multi-agent generation and steering mechanism, and lacks integration with iterative generation loops like SciMON.
revised_idea.methodology: We propose an integrated multi-agent ideation pipeline incorporating latent-probe-based prompt conditioning. To adhere to hardware limits of a single 12GB consumer GPU within a 6-week timeline, we use locally hosted open-weights 4-bit quantized Llama-3-8B-Instruct models without full fine-tuning. Instead of unstable live runtime activation vector manipulation, we extract hidden states from the critic agent during its reasoning phase and apply offline-trained lightweight linear probes to predict explicit novelty tiers. The continuous probed novelty scores are mapped via a discrete translation function into natural prompt prefixes injected into the generator agent's context, pulling outputs away from safe medium-novelty compromises toward high-risk, high-reward conceptual spaces.
revised_idea.expected_contribution: An integrated multi-agent scientific ideation framework leveraging open-weights hidden state probing and lightweight prompt-level conditioning to eliminate medium-novelty bias, yielding research directions with higher technical depth and verified novelty scores without requiring full LLM fine-tuning.
revised_idea.experimental_setup: We utilize a representative subset of 50 background contexts drawn from the RINoBench benchmark and SciMON generation tasks to ensure compute feasibility. We deploy a multi-agent ideation architecture consisting of diverse personas (generator, reviewer, domain expert) using locally hosted Llama-3-8B-Instruct models. We compare our probe-enhanced multi-agent loop against standard multi-agent generation baselines, standalone SciMON configurations, a prompt-only novelty constraint text baseline, and classifier-guided decoding baselines.
revised_idea.evaluation_strategy: We evaluate generated ideas using RINoBench metrics and the Idea Novelty Checker framework. We measure alignment with human expert novelty judgments, distribution variance across novelty tiers to verify mitigation of medium-novelty bias, technical depth scores, and computational footprint analysis tracking latency and memory overhead on the consumer GPU. We also include a falsification baseline to verify whether prompt conditioning yields actual technical depth rather than superficial lexical novelty.
feasibility_assumptions: Access to locally hosted open-weights models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) compatible with a 12GB consumer GPU via 4-bit quantization.
Availability of public RINoBench dataset and SciMON benchmark contexts for evaluation.
Feasibility of completing the 6-week project timeline using frozen base weights and offline-trained lightweight linear probes without full LLM fine-tuning.
Reliance on discrete prompt conditioning derived from a robust fallback mapping function to maintain semantic coherence and avoid VRAM bottlenecks.
